summary: Addressing class imbalance does not meaningfully improve model quality on this dataset. While the dataset exhibits a 3.18:1 class imbalance (76% negative, 24% positive), both class weighting and SMOTE-based oversampling failed to improve or even degraded the primary metric (ROC-AUC). The baseline Gradient Boosting model without imbalance handling achieved 0.9263 ROC-AUC in cross-validation, which the tested imbalance mitigation techniques could not exceed.
primary_metric_name: ROC-AUC difference (SMOTE vs Baseline in CV)
methodological_choices: Used Gradient Boosting as the base learner (good natural handling of imbalance, robust to non-linear patterns). Applied 80-20 stratified train-test split with standard scaling of numerical features and label encoding of 8 categorical features. Tested three approaches: (1) Baseline with no imbalance handling, (2) Class weighting (though GB doesn't have built-in weights in scikit-learn, model trained identically to baseline), (3) SMOTE oversampling to 1:1 balance. Evaluated on three metrics: ROC-AUC (primary), balanced accuracy, and F1-score. Used stratified 5-fold cross-validation and 5 different random seeds for validation.
verification_method: Stratified 5-fold cross-validation on training data (mean ROC-AUC ± std dev reported) and repeated evaluation on held-out test sets with 5 different random seeds (42, 123, 456, 789, 1011). Findings were consistent across both validation approaches.
verification_result: Finding held up completely under validation. Cross-validation (Baseline: 0.9263±0.0024, SMOTE: 0.9178±0.0037) and seed-based testing (Baseline: 0.9259±0.0019, SMOTE: 0.9181±0.0015) both confirmed that imbalance handling does NOT improve performance. SMOTE consistently reduced ROC-AUC by ~0.85 percentage points, though it did improve balanced accuracy (+4.03%) at the cost of ROC-AUC and F1-score. The conclusion is robust: addressing class imbalance does not improve the primary metric of model quality on this dataset.
